tribe: Banu Adi ibn an-Najjar of al-Khazraj — Ansar of Madinah
era: The Boy Who Served Ten Years
teaser: Ten years at his side, and not once was he asked why he had done a thing.

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: A Madinan house that kept losing its men
layers.content:
Anas ibn Malik ibn an-Nadr, of the Banu Adi ibn an-Najjar, a clan of al-Khazraj. Ibn Sa'd, listing the Ansar, does not bother with a title for him. He simply writes: the servant of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

His mother was Umm Sulaym bint Milhan. Her two brothers were Haram and Sulaym ibn Milhan, both at Badr and Uhud, both killed later at Bi'r Ma'unah. His father's sister was ar-Rubayya' bint an-Nadr, whose son Haritha ibn Suraqa was shot through the throat at Badr while looking out from the ranks.

When Haritha was killed his mother came to the Prophet ﷺ and said what a bereaved woman says when she is past politeness: you know what Haritha meant to me — if he is in the Garden I will be patient, and if not, you will see what I do. He answered her, there is not one Garden but many Gardens, and Haritha is in the best of them.

Anas grew up hearing that answer from his own aunt. It is the household he came from: not one of soldiers exactly, but one where the funerals came early and were argued out loud with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the lineage of Banu Adi ibn an-Najjar, Anas named as the servant of the Prophet ﷺ, Haritha ibn Suraqa's death at Badr and his mother's words, narrated from Anas through Thabit al-Bunani

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: His mother handed him over, aged about ten
layers.content:
He never had a conversion in the ordinary sense. He was a child in Madinah when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived there, and his mother was already among the women who had given allegiance. Islam reached him the way a language reaches a boy: before he could weigh it.

What happened instead was a handing over. Umm Sulaym brought her son to the Prophet ﷺ and put him into his service, and she asked him to make du'a for the boy. He said: O Allah, increase his wealth and his children, and bless him in what You give him.

His stepfather was Abu Talhah, Zayd ibn Sahl of the same clan, one of the seventy at the second 'Aqaba, present at Badr, Uhud, the Ditch and every campaign after. Abu Talhah had a voice that carried; the Prophet ﷺ said his voice in the army was better than a thousand men.

So the cost was not paid by Anas. It was paid by his mother, who gave away the only childhood she had to give, and it was paid in advance. She did not ask what the arrangement would do for her son's prospects. She asked for a du'a and let him go.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Du'a — Umm Sulaym asking the Prophet ﷺ to pray for Anas
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Du'a and Book of Manners, narrated by Anas; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, for Abu Talhah's lineage, his presence at 'Aqaba and every battle, and the Prophet's ﷺ words about his voice, narrated from Anas

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: Ten years, and never once a rebuke
layers.content:
This is the sentence the ummah has never let go of. Anas said: I served the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for ten years, and he never once said uff to me. He never said of something I had done, why did you do that, and he never said of something I had left, why did you not do that.

Ten years is enough time to break a dish, lose a message, arrive late, forget. A servant boy in a household of that pressure had every opportunity to be corrected sharply. He was not corrected sharply once.

He told a small story that shows the temperature of it. He was out playing with the other boys when the Prophet ﷺ came by, greeted them, and sent Anas on an errand. He came home late. His mother asked what had kept him. He said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent him somewhere. She asked what for. He said, it is a secret. She did not press. She said: then guard the secret of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

A child, trusted with something confidential, and a mother who reinforced the trust instead of satisfying her own curiosity. That is the whole apprenticeship in one exchange.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, narrated by Anas ibn Malik — the ten years without rebuke, and the errand kept secret
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Manners (al-Adab) and Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, both narrated by Anas ibn Malik

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Seventy reciters sent out, and his uncle among them
layers.content:
People came to the Prophet ﷺ asking for men to teach them the Qur'an and the Sunnah. He sent seventy of the Ansar. Anas describes what those seventy were like at home: they recited and studied by night, and by day they hauled water into the mosque and gathered firewood, sold it, and used the money to feed the men of the Suffah and the poor.

Anas's uncle Haram ibn Milhan was one of them. At Bi'r Ma'unah he went ahead of the party to speak first, on the reasoning that if they granted him safety he could deliver the message, and if not, his companions were close behind. They granted him safety. While he was telling them about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a man came from the side and put a spear through him. Haram said: Allah is greater. I have won, by the Lord of the Ka'bah.

The rest were killed except one lame man who got up the mountain. Anas's other uncle, Sulaym ibn Milhan, was among the dead.

He was a boy of the household that received that news. Then he went back to serving. Neither the tenderness he lived inside nor the grief was theoretical, and he never separated the two in his narrations.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the seventy reciters and Bi'r Ma'unah, narrated from Anas ibn Malik through Thabit al-Bunani and through Ishaq ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Talhah; the entries on Haram ibn Milhan and Sulaym ibn Milhan

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: The du'a came true, and he kept the vial
layers.content:
The du'a his mother asked for was answered in the ordinary visible way. His wealth grew. His descendants ran past a hundred in his own lifetime, children and grandchildren, and he used to count them when he told the story.

He settled in Basra and taught there for decades, and the men who took hadith from him are a large part of why the sunnah of daily life — how the Prophet ﷺ ate, slept, prayed, spoke to children, dealt with servants — survives at the level of detail it does. Not the great public rulings. The texture.

One thing he kept literally. Umm Sulaym had once spread a mat for the Prophet ﷺ to rest on in her house, and while he slept she collected the sweat from his brow into a small bottle. Anas gave instructions that when he died some of it was to be put into the perfume used on his body.

Reports differ on the year he died; 91, 92 and 93 AH are all given. He outlived nearly everyone.

He had one sentence about ten years, and it has done more for the manners of this ummah than most libraries. Nobody was ever told off. That was the method.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Asking Permission (Kitab al-Isti'dhan), narrated by Anas — Umm Sulaym collecting the Prophet's ﷺ sweat, and Anas's instruction about his own embalming
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Du'a and Book of Asking Permission, narrated by Anas ibn Malik; reports differ on the year of his death in Basra

quiz.prompt: How did Anas describe ten years of serving the Prophet ﷺ?

options.text: He was corrected gently but often
He was never once told uff, never asked why he did a thing or why he left it
He was paid a wage from the treasury
He was kept away from the Prophet's ﷺ household affairs

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Manners, and Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, narrated by Anas
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ten years is long enough to break, forget and mislay a great deal. The record is not that he made no mistakes. It is that he was never shamed for one.

quiz.prompt: What did Umm Sulaym ask for when she brought her son to the Prophet ﷺ?

options.text: A position for him among the scribes
A share of the spoils for the household
A du'a — that his wealth and children be increased and blessed
That he be excused from military service

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Du'a, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: She was handing over her only son's childhood. What she requested in return was not a place, a salary or a promise. It was a supplication.

quiz.prompt: When the boy Anas came home late and said the Prophet's ﷺ errand was a secret, what did his mother say?

options.text: She insisted he tell her, as his guardian
She told him to guard the secret of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ
She went to the Prophet ﷺ herself to ask
She forbade him from going out again

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: She had every ordinary right to know. She gave the right up so that her son could be the kind of person a secret could be left with.

quiz.prompt: What did Anas's uncle Haram ibn Milhan say when he was speared at Bi'r Ma'unah?

options.text: 'Tell my sister I did not run'
'Allah is greater. I have won, by the Lord of the Ka'bah'
'O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know'
'I have delivered the message'

quiz.citation: Narrated from Anas ibn Malik through Ishaq ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Talhah — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had gone forward alone precisely so that if it went badly it would go badly for him first. It did, and he called it winning.

quiz.prompt: According to Anas, how did the seventy Ansari reciters support themselves in Madinah before Bi'r Ma'unah?

options.text: They were paid teachers of the Qur'an
They lived from the spoils of Badr
They carried water into the mosque and sold firewood to feed the men of the Suffah and the poor
They were supported by the Muhajirun's trade

quiz.citation: Narrated from Anas ibn Malik through Thabit al-Bunani — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: They studied at night and hauled firewood by day, and the money went to men poorer than themselves. Then they were sent out and killed.

quiz.prompt: Nobody in that household was told off for ten years, and it made a scholar. What does correction usually sound like coming out of you?

options.text: Sharp and immediate, and I think it is efficient
I say nothing and then resent the person
I try for gentle and it comes out heavier than I meant
I have learned to let most small things go entirely

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Manners, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: Note what was not required for the boy to turn out well: no rebuke, no interrogation, no accounting for the errand he mishandled.

quiz.prompt: Umm Sulaym handed over her son and asked only for a du'a. What do you find hardest to hand over to Allah without conditions?

options.text: My children, or the people I am responsible for
My money, plainly
My plan for how my life is supposed to go
My reputation with people who matter to me

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Du'a, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: She did not negotiate a role for him or a place for herself. Whatever she felt about it, the request she made out loud was a du'a.

quiz.prompt: His aunt told the Prophet ﷺ plainly that if her son was not in the Garden he would see what she did. How honest are you with Allah when you are grieving?

options.text: I say the correct things and feel something else
I say exactly what I feel and then worry it was wrong
I go silent, and that is my version of honesty
I have not been tested hard enough to know

quiz.citation: Narrated from Anas ibn Malik — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: She was not reprimanded for how she said it. She was answered: not one Garden but many, and Haritha is in the best of them.

quiz.prompt: Anas is the source for the small domestic detail — how the Prophet ﷺ ate, rested, spoke to children. What do the people who live with you learn about you that others never see?

options.text: The private version is worse than the public one
They are close enough that there is not much difference
The private version is warmer; I am stiff in public
I would rather not have this examined

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Manners, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: The servant of the house is the one witness who cannot be managed. This ummah's picture of the Prophet's ﷺ private manners rests largely on his testimony.

quiz.prompt: He asked for a vial of collected sweat to be put in his own burial perfume. What physical thing do you keep because of who it connects you to?

options.text: Something inherited that I would not sell at any price
Nothing — I am not sentimental about objects
Several things, and I have never examined why
I lost the one that mattered and still think about it

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Asking Permission (Kitab al-Isti'dhan), narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: His mother had collected it while the Prophet ﷺ slept in her house. Seventy or eighty years later her son was still planning what to do with it.
